cards.front: What does a pipe (|) do in a shell?
cards.back: It connects the standard output of the command on its left to the standard input of the command on its right.

cards.front: What is the difference between > and >> ?
cards.back: > writes a command's output to a file, replacing its content; >> appends to the file.

cards.front: How do you send a message to standard error in bash?
cards.back: echo "message" >&2. Errors on stderr stay visible when stdout is redirected or piped.

cards.front: Who expands *.csv in "mv *.csv archive/": mv or the shell?
cards.back: The shell. mv receives the list of matching names; with no match, bash passes the literal *.csv unless nullglob is set.

cards.front: Why write "$file" with quotes?
cards.back: Without quotes, a value with spaces or glob characters is split into several words or expanded. Quotes keep it as one argument.

cards.front: What does set -euo pipefail do?
cards.back: -e exits on many command failures, with exceptions for conditionals and command lists; handle expected failures explicitly, -u treats unset variables as errors, pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any command in it fails.

cards.front: How do you read the exit code of the last command, and what does 0 mean?
cards.back: $? holds it; 0 means success, anything else a failure.

cards.front: What does [ -s "$file" ] test?
cards.back: That the file exists and has a size greater than zero.

cards.front: What do grep -c, -i, -v and -r do?
cards.back: -c counts matching lines, -i ignores case, -v keeps the lines that do not match, -r searches folders recursively.

cards.front: Why is uniq -c usually preceded by sort?
cards.back: uniq only merges adjacent equal lines; sort puts equal lines next to each other first.

cards.front: What does mkdir -p a/b/c do?
cards.back: Creates a, a/b and a/b/c as needed, and does not fail if they already exist.

cards.front: How does a PowerShell pipeline differ from a bash pipeline?
cards.back: PowerShell passes objects between commands (Get-ChildItem | Where-Object Length -gt 0), bash passes text.

cards.front: What are the working tree, the index and the repository in Git?
cards.back: The working tree holds your files; the index (staging area) holds what the next commit will contain; the repository holds the commits.

cards.front: What does git add do?
cards.back: It copies the current content of a file into the index, to be included in the next commit.

cards.front: What is the difference between git diff and git diff --staged?
cards.back: git diff shows changes not yet staged; git diff --staged shows staged changes that the next commit will record.

cards.front: What does a Git commit contain?
cards.back: A snapshot of the staged tree, its parent commit(s), an author, a committer, a date and a message, all identified by a hash.

cards.front: What is a Git branch?
cards.back: A movable name that points to one commit. Committing on it moves it forward to the new commit.

cards.front: What is HEAD?
cards.back: The pointer to what you have checked out: usually the current branch, or a commit directly in detached HEAD state.

cards.front: Does adding a file to .gitignore remove it from the repository?
cards.back: No. .gitignore only stops untracked files from being added. A tracked file must be removed with git rm --cached, and it stays in older commits.

cards.front: What is the difference between a lightweight and an annotated tag?
cards.back: A lightweight tag is just a name for a commit; an annotated tag (git tag -a) is an object with its own author, date and message.

cards.front: What does a Conventional Commits message look like?
cards.back: type(scope): summary, for example "fix(loader): skip empty files". Common types are feat, fix, docs, refactor, test and chore.

cards.front: What is a fast-forward merge?
cards.back: When the target branch has no commits of its own since the branches split, Git moves its pointer forward without creating a merge commit.

cards.front: What is special about a merge commit?
cards.back: It has two (or more) parents, joining the histories of the merged branches without rewriting them.

cards.front: What does git rebase main do on a feature branch?
cards.back: It replays the feature commits on top of main, creating new commits with new hashes, for a linear history.

cards.front: Why not rebase commits that others have already pulled?
cards.back: Rebase replaces them with new commits; collaborators who built on the old ones end up with duplicated or conflicting history.

cards.front: What do <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> mean in a file?
cards.back: Conflict markers: the part between <<<<<<< and ======= is one side, between ======= and >>>>>>> the other. Edit to the final content, remove them, then git add.

cards.front: How do you give up on a merge or rebase in progress?
cards.back: git merge --abort or git rebase --abort return to the state before it started.

cards.front: What does git cherry-pick <hash> do?
cards.back: Applies the changes of that one commit on top of the current branch as a new commit.

cards.front: How do you find a commit after a git reset --hard or a deleted branch?
cards.back: git reflog lists where HEAD has been; create a branch at the lost commit with git branch rescued <hash>.

cards.front: What does git stash do?
cards.back: Saves uncommitted changes as a stash entry and cleans the working tree; git stash apply or pop brings them back.
